name: Charlotte Smith
chief_complaint: Runny nose and cough for 3 days
opening_statement: My daughter Charlotte has had a runny nose and cough for the past few days. She's been a bit irritable and not eating as well as usual.
emotional_baseline: Parent appears mildly concerned but calm. Charlotte is alert but appears mildly uncomfortable, with occasional coughing and nasal discharge.

symptoms.character: Clear, watery discharge initially, now slightly thicker and white

rag_citations.quote: Viral upper respiratory tract infections in children typically present with clear or mucopurulent rhinorrhea lasting 5-10 days
Acute cough in children under 3 years is most commonly due to viral URTI, characterized by dry cough worsening at night due to postnasal drip

symptoms.severity: Mild - eating about 50-60% of normal intake
symptoms.character: Decreased interest in food and shorter feeding duration

rag_citations.reference: Viral URTI in infants and toddlers - Clinical features
rag_citations.quote: Young children with viral URTI commonly experience reduced oral intake due to nasal congestion and general malaise, though fluid intake typically remains adequate

rag_citations.reference: Fever in children - Assessment and management
rag_citations.quote: Low-grade fever (<38.5°C) in young children with URTI symptoms is typical of viral infection and does not require routine antipyretic therapy unless causing discomfort

past_medical_history.details: Normal vaginal delivery, birth weight 3.2kg, no complications
Up to date with Australian National Immunisation Program schedule - 2, 4, 6, 12 months completed

medications.name: Paracetamol (acetaminophen)
medications.pbs_restriction: S3 Pharmacy Medicine - no PBS restriction for pediatric formulations

allergies: No known drug allergies (NKDA). No food allergies.
family_history: Non-contributory. No family history of asthma, atopy, or immunodeficiency. Both parents well. One older sibling (4 years) currently healthy.

social_history.living_situation: Lives with both parents and 4-year-old brother in suburban home
social_history.daycare: Attends daycare 3 days per week (recent viral illness circulating)
social_history.developmental: Meeting all developmental milestones appropriately for age
social_history.parental_concerns: Parents concerned about cough and reduced eating, but child still playful and interactive

general.appearance: Alert, interactive child with mild nasal discharge
general.hydration_status: Well hydrated - normal skin turgor, moist mucous membranes

heent.ears: Tympanic membranes mobile, no erythema or effusion bilaterally
heent.nose: Clear rhinorrhea, mildly congested nasal mucosa, no purulent discharge
heent.throat: Mildly erythematous posterior pharynx, no tonsillar exudate, no peritonsillar swelling
heent.lymph_nodes: Small (<1cm) mobile anterior cervical lymph nodes bilaterally - reactive

respiratory.inspection: No respiratory distress, no nasal flaring, no intercostal recession
respiratory.auscultation: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no wheeze, no crackles, good air entry

cardiovascular.auscultation: Dual heart sounds, no murmurs, regular rhythm

neurological.signs_of_meningism: None - no neck stiffness, normal activity level

optional.indication: Not routinely indicated for uncomplicated viral URTI in otherwise healthy child
optional.expected_result: If performed, would likely show common respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, coronavirus, RSV)
optional.mbs_item: MBS 69494 (respiratory virus PCR panel) - restricted use, not PBS funded for simple URTI

red_flags_requiring_investigation: Poor feeding with <50% normal intake AND reduced urine output

interventions: Reassurance - self-limiting condition, expected duration 5-10 days
Maintain adequate hydration - encourage frequent small fluid intake
Saline nasal drops/spray for nasal congestion (can use before feeds)
Elevate head of cot/bed to reduce postnasal drip
Paracetamol 15mg/kg Q4-6H PRN for fever >38.5°C or significant discomfort (maximum 4 doses/24 hours)
Ibuprofen 10mg/kg Q6-8H PRN as alternative/adjunct if >3 months old
expected_management.australian_guidance: eTG Complete - Acute upper respiratory tract infections in children

interventions: Return if fever persists >3 days or temperature >39°C
Return if breathing becomes difficult (fast breathing, noisy breathing, chest recession)
Return if child becomes lethargic or difficult to rouse
Return if fluid intake drops significantly or reduced wet nappies (<4/day)
Expected improvement in 5-7 days; cough may persist up to 3 weeks
expected_management.australian_guidance: AMC Clinical Examination - Pediatric red flags

expected_management.category: What NOT to Do (Critical for AMC Exam)
interventions: NO antibiotics - viral etiology, antibiotics ineffective and increase resistance
NO cough suppressants in children <6 years (not recommended, limited evidence)
NO over-the-counter cold and flu medications <6 years (TGA restriction)
NO aspirin in children (Reye syndrome risk)
NO decongestants in children <6 years (cardiovascular side effects)
expected_management.australian_guidance: TGA safety alerts - Pediatric cough and cold medicines

interventions: Routine follow-up not required if improving as expected
If cough persists >3-4 weeks, review to exclude post-viral cough or other etiology
Counsel parents about infection control (hand hygiene, tissue disposal) to prevent spread to siblings

critical_errors.error: Prescribing antibiotics for uncomplicated viral URTI
critical_errors.rationale: Viral etiology - antibiotics ineffective, contribute to antimicrobial resistance, and cause unnecessary adverse effects. No features of bacterial co-infection present.

rag_citation.reference: Acute upper respiratory tract infections - Antibiotic stewardship
rag_citation.quote: Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral URTI in children. Features requiring antibiotics include persistent fever >3 days, purulent nasal discharge >10 days, or signs of bacterial sinusitis/otitis media.

critical_errors.error: Recommending OTC cough and cold medications
critical_errors.rationale: TGA restriction for children <6 years due to lack of efficacy and risk of cardiovascular side effects. This is a medication safety issue.

rag_citation.reference: Cough and cold medicines - Not for young children
rag_citation.quote: Over-the-counter cough and cold medicines should not be given to children under 6 years of age. These products have not been shown to be effective in children and may cause serious side effects.

critical_errors.error: Failing to provide safety netting advice
critical_errors.rationale: Critical for patient safety - parents must know when to return if child deteriorates. Essential component of AMC clinical exam communication skills.

rag_citation.reference: Communication and patient safety - Safety netting
rag_citation.quote: Candidates must provide clear safety netting advice, including specific red flag symptoms requiring urgent review, particularly for pediatric presentations.

critical_errors.error: Not addressing parental concerns about reduced eating
critical_errors.rationale: Failure to address ICE (Ideas, Concerns, Expectations). Parents need reassurance that reduced appetite is expected with viral URTI and guidance on maintaining hydration.

rag_citation.quote: Candidates must elicit and address patient/parent concerns, providing evidence-based reassurance where appropriate.

critical_errors.error: Ordering unnecessary investigations (e.g., nasopharyngeal viral PCR)
critical_errors.rationale: Not indicated for uncomplicated viral URTI - does not change management, increases healthcare costs, and causes unnecessary discomfort to child.

rag_citation.quote: Viral PCR testing is not routinely indicated for uncomplicated URTI in immunocompetent children as results do not alter clinical management.

critical_errors.rationale: Contraindicated in children <16 years due to Reye syndrome risk. This is a medication safety issue and automatic fail in AMC exam.

rag_citation.quote: Aspirin must not be used in children under 16 years due to the risk of Reye syndrome, a rare but potentially fatal condition.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP (Pediatrics), APLS Instructor, 15 years experience in general pediatrics
fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent representation of common pediatric presentation. Age-appropriate vital signs, realistic parental concerns, and clear learning points around antibiotic stewardship and TGA restrictions. Critical errors appropriately calibrated for AMC exam - antibiotic prescription and aspirin use are definite auto-fails. Safety netting advice is essential skill to assess.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: None - scenario is clinically sound and educationally valuable for AMC preparation.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP (General Medicine), AMC Clinical Exam Assessor, 12 years experience
fracp_reviews.comments: Appropriate difficulty level for 'Easy' category - straightforward diagnosis with no comorbidities. Good emphasis on what NOT to do, which is critical for AMC exam success. RAG citations appropriately reference Australian guidelines (eTG, TGA) rather than international sources. Opening statement and emotional baseline help candidates practice communication skills in realistic context.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: Consider adding specific MBS item numbers for GP consultation to reinforce Australian healthcare context, though not essential for clinical accuracy.

learning_objectives.objective: Differentiate viral URTI from bacterial infection requiring antibiotics
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: HIGH - antibiotic stewardship is frequently tested in AMC clinical exam
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: Viral URTI features: low-grade fever, clear/white rhinorrhea, dry cough, self-limiting course. Bacterial infection features: high fever >3 days, purulent discharge >10 days, unilateral facial pain (sinusitis), otalgia with bulging TM (otitis media).

learning_objectives.objective: Understand TGA restrictions on pediatric cough and cold medications
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: HIGH - medication safety is core AMC competency
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: OTC cough/cold medicines contraindicated <6 years due to lack of efficacy and risk of serious cardiovascular/neurological side effects. Candidates must know Australian-specific regulations.

learning_objectives.objective: Provide appropriate safety netting advice for pediatric presentations
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: CRITICAL - essential communication skill assessed in all AMC clinical stations
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: Parents must know specific red flags: persistent high fever >3 days, respiratory distress (tachypnea, recession), lethargy, poor feeding with dehydration signs. Clear instructions prevent delayed representation and improve patient safety.

learning_objectives.objective: Recognize normal vital signs and examination findings in 2-year-old child
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: Normal HR 80-130 bpm, RR 20-30/min, temp <37.5°C. Anterior fontanelle closes 12-18 months. Reactive lymphadenopathy (<1cm, mobile) is normal with viral URTI.

learning_objectives.objective: Apply supportive care principles for self-limiting viral illness
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: HIGH - demonstrates clinical judgement and avoiding over-investigation/treatment
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: Supportive care (hydration, antipyretics PRN, saline nasal drops) is evidence-based management. Avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and investigations shows good stewardship and cost-effective practice.

learning_objectives.objective: Address parental concerns using ICE (Ideas, Concerns, Expectations) framework
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: HIGH - communication skills domain in AMC exam
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: Parents concerned about reduced eating - provide reassurance that this is expected with nasal congestion, emphasize importance of maintaining hydration, and give practical advice (smaller frequent meals, elevate head during feeds).

learning_objectives.objective: Understand contraindications to aspirin in children (Reye syndrome)
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: CRITICAL - medication safety, potential auto-fail if prescribed
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: Aspirin contraindicated <16 years due to Reye syndrome risk (acute encephalopathy + hepatic failure). Use paracetamol or ibuprofen for antipyretic therapy instead.

learning_objectives.objective: Recognize when investigations are NOT indicated (Choosing Wisely principles)
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: MEDIUM - resource stewardship and evidence-based practice
learning_objectives.clinical_reasoning: Viral PCR does not change management in uncomplicated URTI. Avoiding unnecessary tests reduces healthcare costs, patient discomfort, and demonstrates clinical judgement aligned with Choosing Wisely Australia guidelines.
